column3: By the account of the Haran Gawaita, Nasoraean disciples of John the Baptist leave Jerusalem for Haran or Hauran, then the Median hills and southern Mesopotamia; scholars dispute whether the origin lay in Israel or in Mesopotamia.

The colophons of the Left Ginza attest Mandaeans in the late Parthian Empire, where they flourish under royal protection until the Sasanian emperor Bahram I and his high priest Kartir persecute non-Zoroastrians.
At the Muslim conquest of Mesopotamia their leader Anush bar Danqa is said to have shown the Ginza Rabba to the Muslim authorities; the account is likely apocryphal.
Al-Hasan ibn Bahlul, citing the vizier ibn Muqla, is the earliest source to call the Mandaeans Sabians, the name of the Quran's People of the Book.
The Dominican Riccoldo da Monte di Croce meets the Mandaeans in Mesopotamia, possibly the first European source on the religion.

Carmelite missionaries at Basra call the Mandaeans Christians of Saint John; in 1831 cholera at Shushtar destroys most of the religious authorities, and the priesthood is reestablished at Suq al-Shuyukh.
After the invasion of 2003 many Mandaeans flee Iraq, most to Iran, Syria and Jordan; by 2007 about 5,000 remain in Iraq.
Diaspora communities grow in Sweden, the Netherlands, Germany, Canada, New Zealand, the UK, the United States and above all Australia, where around 10,000 live.
